articles.title: Grammy-Winning Superstar, 40, Welcomes First Child
articles.description: Kevin Mazur / Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Lady Gaga is enjoying some quiet time with her Baby Gaga. Page Six is reporting that the 40-year-old music superstar has welcomed her first child with fiancé Michael Polansky, 42, and they’ve got the pictures to prove it. Shortly after posting the news that the 16-time Grammy winner had welcomed a child into their growing family, the outlet shared exclusive photos of Gaga (real name: Stefani Germanotta) and Polansky walking in Northern California with the newborn. The Oscar winner was last spotted in public a month ago, again in Northern California, where she took a selfie with a fan. Neither she nor her entrepreneur fiancé has shared any details about the child, but Gaga has been very open about her desire to become a mom. In a New York Times interview published in March 2025, she said, “I’m excited to be a mom. I used to have a lot of apprehension about it. The thing that’s the most important to me is to not force my children to live a life that they are not choosing. So the more that we can give them space to discover who they are on their own, that’s the thing that I believe in the most.” The Daily Beast has reached out to Lady Gaga’s representative for comment. articles.title: Why Are Fortnite’s Player Numbers Falling So Hard This Season?
articles.description: Ever since Fortnite started publicly posting player numbers back in 2023, the doomsayers have come out in full force any time there's a decline in concurrent or average player numbers. We're in exactly one of those situations right now, as player counts for the game's main mode, Battle Royale, have fallen significantly since Chapter 7 Season 4 started on August 14. After the summer season saw a big bump in engagement, thanks to some combination of the sprite-focused gameplay and the nearly entirely new map that Epic dropped at the start of Season 3, player counts have been heading back towards the sort of numbers we saw in Season 1 and 2. In other words: Not great, Bob! According to fortnite.gg, which collates players numbers from the Fortnite API , the average number of players in BR is down 37% in September from August so far. We had the usual big spike of players right at the start of Season 4 in the middle of August, but the falloff has been steady ever since, and the "Fortnite is dead" crowd has emerged once again. But what's going on, really? Is Fortnite dying, or is this just the usual seasonal ebb and flow of player traffic? It's not an easy question to answer from the outside, even with the data we have. To get a better idea of what's going on, we looked at four potential factors. School's back This is one of the more obvious factors we could blame–the kids and college students who had lots of free time to game all day during the summer are now busy with school again. Typically, though, the biggest difference in terms of player numbers when comparing the summer versus. the rest of the year is not that more people are playing, but that they're playing at all hours instead of being concentrated at peak times. For most of the year, there's a big difference in the number of concurrent players between peak hours and the middle of the night, but during the summer, the highs and the lows each day are closer together. So being back in school doesn't seem to stop people from playing--it just makes them play more in the evening. The data we have for past fall seasons supports this idea, as average numbers largely stayed flat between the summer and fall seasons in 2023, and the averages took a nice jump up for the Marvel-themed Chapter 5 Season 4 in 2024. Player numbers have fallen pretty hard both in Chapter 6 Season 4 and in this year's gaming-focused Chapter 7 Season 4, but it seems like we'll need something other than school schedules to blame for that. Keeping the sprites Fortnite introduced sprites as the main gameplay gimmick in Chapter 7 Season 3, and since player engagement was way up, Epic decided to keep them around in Season 4. This is pretty much unheard of in modern Fortnite, where each season introduces some major new tweak to the Battle Royale formula to keep it fresh, before shuffling it out the door for something new when the season ends. It's not hard to understand the thinking there, however. Fortnite's player counts had been dropping steadily during Chapter 7, to some of the game's lowest numbers ever in Season 2. Then, the sprite-collection gameplay was added for Season 3 alongside a new map, and player numbers went back up. Clearly, the people liked that mechanic, and it was something the powers-that-be could point to as being "something that works." But there's a reason they basically never keep the same gimmick two seasons in a row–by the end of the season, players are usually over whatever the bit is and ready for something new. That was certainly the case even with sprites as we got to the end of Season 3, but Epic pushed ahead with a new batch of sprites anyway. Anecdotally, players in my matches rarely seem to engage with the sprite-collecting mechanics in the new season--I rarely hear extractors going off in matches anymore, and my random-fill teammates and I tend to treat the sprites as just another type of loot to find rather than a core mechanic. It wasn't like that at any point during Season 3, even in my overly sweaty matches--folks were grinding those sprites to the very end last season. Too many gimmicks Season 4 has a bit of an identity crisis, because it introduced an entirely new season gimmick while also keeping the one from last season. In a normal season of Fortnite, the new map changes, the override consoles--which let players change the rules of the game mid-match--and the new loot would be more than enough to shake things up. But in Season 4 we have all that and a new set of sprites, each with its own new ability. Having two seasons' worth of gimmicks at the same time has made Season 4 feel harder to comprehend, because it's so unnecessarily busy. With so much going on, it's easy to lose a fight without really understanding what happened or why. It's exactly the kind of situation that overwhelms a lot of players, which then inspires a new generation of Redditors to claim everyone who beats them in a fight is cheating because they're frustrated. And since the sprite-collection gameplay is more appealing to those casual players who are put off by the overly complicated gameplay, Season 4 ends up feeling overstimulating and lacking cohesion. We saw the same thing happen in the Helldivers-like Chapter 6 Season 4, when the map was filled with alien bugs that made it more difficult to track other players. The numbers fell pretty hard that season, too. They've been relying too much on engagement farming In 2026, Fortnite has been trying some new techniques for drumming up engagement, the most notable being the Power Hours the game runs in Battle Royale each weekend, which adds some wacky quirks to gameplay, like big head mode, and makes it easier to find and extract sprites. It's essentially a marketing tactic to coerce people to play at a specific time each Saturday so they can get a nice big spike in the concurrent player count, and drag the average player numbers for the rest of the week upward a little bit. But that sort of thing is a bald manipulation, a new layer of FOMO on a game that already has too many of them. At some point, this kind of thing can easily change from being a nice bonus to feeling like an obligation, especially if they continue to center these events around sprites, which--again--was last season's gimmick, instead of coming up with new ideas for them. Maybe we've already reached that point--the August 29 and September 5 Power Hours were the only ones to draw under a million players since the beginning of June, when Epic first started doing them. All this means that the rest of the year will be pivotal for Fortnite. There are several big opportunities for the numbers to recover in the next few months--Fortnitemares in October, the expected mini-season in November, and the start of Chapter 8 in December. The last time Fortnite was able to generate a big, sustained spike in players was in 2023, with the original OG season and the start of Chapter 5. But if Epic wants to pull off that sort of recovery this year, especially with the juggernaut that is GTA 6 looming in November, it'll have to come up with something genuinely special that people actually want to play without having to be coerced into it.

articles.title: New FPS Wardogs Is Dominating Steam Charts, And You Could Get It At A Discount Already
articles.description: I pride myself on spotting upcoming games I’ll enjoy. I’ve had plenty of family and friends ask me what titles they should potentially buy in the near future. However, as far as I know, I had zero knowledge of Wardogs before its early access release. With the FPS game suddenly blowing up on Steam and reaching the #4 spot on the Steam concurrent charts on launch day, you can guarantee I wasn’t just making a surprised Pikachu face; I was intrigued. Now, if you want to jump into the latest hit, Fanatical has it at an excellent discount, beating out the listed price on Steam. Like many, I’m twiddling my thumbs and waiting for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and, of course, a small little game called Grand Theft Auto VI. Sure, plenty is coming up, but the thrills of an excellent shooter? Well, I’m craving it right now. Bringing a more tactical experience, closer to Arma, Hell Let Loose, or Squad than Call of Duty and other arcade-style shooters, Wardogs has definitely given me something to keep me occupied. After playing the tutorial, which teaches you the mechanics of each match—and rewards you with an achievement for punching a guy you just revived; don’t ask me how I know—you’ll be given the chance to dive into a match. The main goal is simple: You and your team need to occupy the control zone for as long as possible, and the first team to reach 100 points wins the match. Sound simple enough? https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v1ISv_h_qXY Of course, it’s not that simple. A volley of bullets will frequently be coming at you, and if you and your team die, reviving isn’t as simple as jumping straight back into battle. Making your way back to the zone can be time-consuming. Fortunately, you don’t just have your guns to kill the enemy team with. You also have special tools, like hammers, which can help you build defenses. Word of warning: You’ll need a forward operating base to build some of the bigger, better pieces of cover. Unsurprisingly, as an early access game from a smaller studio, it’s not as polished as your Battlefield entries or that pesky ol’ Call of Duty that releases every year, but it manages to capture the intensity that makes FPS games one of my favorite genres. That constant tug-of-war between your faction and the other two makes every match feel distinct, violent, and just chaotic fun, especially when things get towards the end and the score is neck-and-neck. With Wardogs out now, you can grab a Steam key for Wardogs for just $32.79 / £30.33 at Fanatical , an 18% discount. You'll have it in your Steam library, with no extra launchers to download. Hopefully, I’ll see you in a match, and we can work together. If we’re on opposing sides, please go easy on me. Just because I love FPS games doesn’t mean I’m actually good at them.
